snapshot.title: UPSC History: Gandhi's Arrival & Early Satyagrahas
snapshot.exam_hook: 🏔️ UPSC History Hook: 1915: Return. 1917: Champaran (Indigo). 1918: Ahmedabad (Mill/Hunger). 1918: Kheda (Revenue). Gokhale: Guru. C-A-K sequence.

quick_notes.title: Gandhi in South Africa (Brief)
quick_notes.detail: Techniques developed: Satyagraha, Ahimsa. Founded Natal Indian Congress, Tolstoy Farm. 1915: Returned to India on Jan 9 (Pravasi Bharatiya Divas). G.K. Gokhale was his political mentor.
quick_notes.explanation: While living in South Africa, Gandhi developed two key methods of protest: Satyagraha, which means holding firmly to truth through nonviolent resistance, and Ahimsa, meaning nonviolence or avoiding harm to any living being. He also founded the Natal Indian Congress, a political organization that united Indians in South Africa to fight for their rights, and established Tolstoy Farm, a self-sufficient community where his followers lived and practiced simple, cooperative living. Gandhi returned to India on January 9, 1915, a date now celebrated in India as Pravasi Bharatiya Divas, or Overseas Indian Day, to honor his return. His political mentor was Gopal Krishna Gokhale, an Indian leader who guided him in his early political work.

quick_notes.title: Champaran Satyagraha (1917 - First Civil Disobedience)
quick_notes.detail: Bihar. Issue : Tinkathia system (peasants forced to grow Indigo on 3/20th of land). Invited by Rajkumar Shukla. Result : Indigo commission formed, Tinkathia abolished.
quick_notes.explanation: Mahatma Gandhi was invited to Champaran, a district in Bihar, by a local farmer named Rajkumar Shukla to help peasants who were suffering under the Tinkathia system. The Tinkathia system was a British law that forced peasants to grow Indigo, a plant used for blue dye, on three out of every twenty parts (3/20th) of their land, even if it was not profitable for them. Civil Disobedience is the act of peacefully refusing to obey a specific law or government order that is considered unjust. Gandhi launched the first Civil Disobedience in India by refusing to leave Champaran when ordered by the British authorities. As a result of the protests, the British government set up an Indigo Commission to investigate the farmers complaints, and the Tinkathia system was legally abolished.

quick_notes.title: Ahmedabad Mill Strike (1918 - First Hunger Strike)
quick_notes.detail: Issue: Discontinuation of "Plague Bonus". Gandhi used hunger strike as a weapon. Result : Workers got 35% wage hike.
quick_notes.explanation: In 1918, textile mill workers in Ahmedabad were demanding a 35% wage increase because the mills had stopped paying a "Plague Bonus," which was extra money given to workers during a plague outbreak to keep them working despite the health risk. Mahatma Gandhi, who was already a leader in India's freedom movement, stepped in to support the workers. When the mill owners refused to negotiate, Gandhi used a new method called a "hunger strike," where he refused to eat food until an agreement was reached. This was the first time Gandhi used a hunger strike as a weapon for a labor dispute. The result was that the workers got their demanded 35% wage hike, showing that nonviolent protest could force employers to give in. This event is important because it introduced the hunger strike as a powerful tool for social and political change in India.

quick_notes.title: Kheda Satyagraha (1918 - First Non-Cooperation)
quick_notes.detail: Gujarat. Issue : Crop failure but British demanded full revenue. Result : Government agreed to collect revenue only from those who could pay.
quick_notes.explanation: The Kheda Satyagraha was a protest that took place in 1918 in the Kheda district of Gujarat, a state in western India. The issue was that crops had failed due to heavy rains, but the British colonial government still demanded that farmers pay the full land revenue, which is the tax they had to pay for using the land. Mahatma Gandhi and other leaders, including Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, organized the farmers to refuse to pay the tax, using non-cooperation, which means peacefully refusing to follow an unjust law. The result of this protest was that the government agreed to collect the revenue only from those farmers who could actually afford to pay, while those who were too poor were exempted. This was one of the first successful mass movements led by Gandhi in India, and it showed that peaceful resistance could force the British to change their policies.

quick_notes.title: Core Philosophy
quick_notes.detail: Satyagraha (Passive resistance based on truth). Ahimsa (Non-violence). Sarvodaya (Upliftment of all). Constructive work (Khadi, Hindu-Muslim unity, untouchability removal).
quick_notes.explanation: The core philosophy of Mahatma Gandhi's approach is based on four main principles. Satyagraha means passive resistance rooted in truth, where people oppose injustice without using violence. Ahimsa is the principle of non-violence, meaning you avoid harming any living being in thought or action. Sarvodaya means upliftment of all, or the welfare of every person in society. Constructive work refers to practical actions for social reform, such as making Khadi (hand-spun cloth), promoting Hindu-Muslim unity, and removing the practice of untouchability (discrimination against certain groups based on caste). These ideas together formed the foundation of Gandhi's movement for India's independence.

topic_title: UPSC History: Gandhi's Arrival & Early Satyagrahas
lesson_intro: Today we study the 'Entry of the Mahatma'. After two decades in South Africa, M.K. Gandhi returned to India in 1915. He didn't join politics immediately; instead, he traveled and tested his weapon of 'Satyagraha' (Truth-Force) in three localized struggles: Champaran, Kheda, and Ahmedabad. These 'Triple Victories' established him as a leader of the masses. For UPSC, mastering the 'Sequence' and 'Issues' of these three struggles is a Prelims favorite. Let's trace the birth of Gandhian politics today.
